details.intro:
The Ethiopic Death of Aaron (Mota Aron, CAVT 143) is a translation, through Arabic, of Jacob of Serugh’s Syriac verse homily On the Death of Aaron (B2 239 = B1 361 = A 5). It circulated among Ethiopian Orthodox Christians and passed to the Betä Ǝsraʾel (Ethiopian Jews).

Earlier scholars (Wurmbrand, Schwarzbaum, Phenix) held that the Ethiopic diverges widely from the Syriac. Butts (2020) shows this is true only of the Betä Ǝsraʾel text type edited by Wurmbrand. The earliest Ethiopic layer (EMML 1939) closely follows its Arabic Vorlage, and the Arabic follows the Syriac. The Faitlovitch Eth. 16 text is a later rewriting that removes Christian language, such as the line on “the Son who will be born.”
details.provenance:
Original language: Syriac (Jacob of Serugh, d. 521), with at least four Syriac text types.
Transmission: Syriac → Arabic (at least two text types; the Ethiopic derives from the Strasbourg / Paris ar. 265 type) → Geʿez → Betä Ǝsraʾel rewriting.
Edition status: only the Betä Ǝsraʾel text of Faitlovitch Eth. 16 is edited (Wurmbrand 1961, Hebrew; French tr. Kaplan 1990). Aaron M. Butts and Michael Hensley are editing both the Christian and the Betä Ǝsraʾel versions, expected in 2027 (Personal communication, A. M. Butts to K. Penner, 28 November 2026.). Butts (2020) earlier announced an edition of EMML 1939 with Reese Hartmann, Dawit Muluneh and Yuening Rao.
details.manuscripts:
• Ethiopic (Christian): EMML 1939 (14th–15th c.); Qorqor Maryam (Gärʿalta) C3-IV-328 (1417–1422), fols. 184r–196v (identified by Ted Erho; not imaged).
  • Ethiopic (Betä Ǝsraʾel): Tel Aviv University, Faitlovitch Eth. 8 (late 19th–early 20th c.), fols. 15r–40r (close to EMML 1939); Faitlovitch Eth. 16 (20th c.), pp. 1–24 (rewritten text type).
  • Arabic (Vorlage type): Strasbourg 4.180 = ar. 33 (16th c.), fols. 99v–113v; Paris, BnF ar. 265 (17th c.), fols. 39v–49r; Vatican, Borg. ar. 200 (19th c.), pp. 334–340; Ḥomṣ, Syriac Orthodox Archdiocese 22 (19th c.), fols. 250r–261r.
  • Arabic (other type): Paris, BnF ar. 153 (17th c.), fols. 470b–478a; Ḥomṣ, Syriac Orthodox Archdiocese 2 (19th c.), fols. 199v–208v.
